events.content_detail:
# Putin makes rare admission of fuel shortages caused by Ukrainian strikes

![](https://static.files.bbci.co.uk/bbcdotcom/web/20260625-085147-1c51ce95ba-web-3.11.1-1/grey-placeholder.png)
![EPA Putin sat at a desk](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/news/480/cpsprodpb/5d81/live/801dc920-73d5-11f1-b1db-af71d47507d6.jpg.webp)

In Russia, the impact of Ukraine's missile and drone strikes on energy infrastructure from Moscow to the Black Sea and beyond has long been evident.

Queues at petrol stations. Fuel rationing widespread. Refineries hit. Drivers in the Russia-annexed [Ukrainian peninsula of Crimea banned from filling their tanks](https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cy06495y2lko) so priority can be given to military vehicles.

But such is the gravity of the situation it has now been explicitly acknowledged by President Vladimir Putin for the first time.

Over the weekend, Russia's president discussed the crisis with senior officials and oil executives. And in public remarks, he was unusually frank.

"You're well aware that problems persist for both motorists and businesses," he told the meeting. "Unfortunately, there are still queues at petrol stations, and finding the right grade of petrol isn't always easy."

He also mentioned the difficulties faced by the agricultural industry and said the harvest "depended on" the fuel supply schedule being met.

According to independent Russian outlet Mediazona, 56 Russian regions are currently enforcing fuel restrictions.

On the streets of Moscow, disgruntled drivers wait patiently for gasoline in a long line of cars and trucks amid an acute national shortage. # Book Review - China and the Global Economic Order

![](/sites/default/files/2018-02/profit-chart.svg)
![China and the Global Economic Order](/sites/default/files/styles/node_landscape/public/images/blog/CGEO.jpg?itok=OI1P55QM "China and the Global Economic Order")

### ***China and the Global Economic Order*** **by Gregory T. Chin and Kevin P. Gallagher. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, Elements in Global China, 2025. 81 pp., £55 hardcover 978-1-009-50908-4, £18 paperback 978-1-009-50907-7; $25 e-book 978-1-009-50906-0, Open access Cambridge Core**

This timely, short book by two leading scholars of China and global economic governance brings together a large body of their individual and coauthored work (together and with others), along with the work of many others in this area. The concise format and accessible writing make the book perfect for undergraduate and graduate courses that address China and the global financial system. It has enough empirical detail and reference to the scholarly literature for scholars to find the book useful as a valuable introduction to the field.

Despite the book’s title, readers should be aware that the work focuses exclusively on China and global financial governance rather than on global economic governance, more broadly. This is not a criticism of the book. After all, global financial governance is a vast, important terrain of *realpolitik*, and most readers
